The life cycle of Rhithrogena semicolorata begins with minute eggs, each measuring 0.0185 centimeters  in length, a dimension that reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the developing embryo prior to hatching. At a controlled water temperature of 8.4 °C [T = 8.4 °C], the period from oviposition to the emergence of the first feeding larva spans 57.7 days [ab = 57.7 days], a duration that aligns with the slow developmental rates typical of early-season stonefly recruits in cool, well-oxygenated streams. Upon the transition to active feeding, the newly hatched nymph begins a prolonged period of exogenous growth, progressing through multiple instars while exploiting periphyton and organic detritus deposited among the gravel substrates of its preferred montane habitats. The total number of eggs produced by a single female across her lifetime, measured at 1,775.0 eggs  when reared under a thermal regime of 8.6 °C [T = 8.6 °C], underscores a reproductive strategy that prioritizes high fecundity over large individual offspring size.

As nymphal development proceeds toward the final larval instar, individuals attain a maximum body length of 1.15 centimeters , a measurement that characterizes the late-stage nymph just prior to the metamorphic transformations that culminate in adult emergence. This weight is largely composed of structural protein and stored lipids that will sustain the insect through the non-feeding subimago stage. The nymphs exhibit a pronounced univoltine phenology, with the duration of the entire aquatic phase being heavily modulated by local thermal conditions; in many populations, growth slows considerably during winter months, resulting in a prolonged development period that extends well into the spring of the following year before the final moult to the winged adult.

This relatively brief pre-reproductive period within the overall larval phase indicates that reproductive competence is achieved well before the final moult, allowing the female to emerge with a complement of mature oocytes ready for fertilization.

The adult portion of the life span is remarkably compressed, a common trait among ephemeropterans that prioritizes rapid mating and oviposition. At 8.5 °C [T = 8.5 °C], the total longevity of the winged imago is 7.0 days [am = 7.0 days], during which the sole function of the adult is to locate a mate, engage in the characteristic aerial swarming behaviour, and deposit eggs. The marked discrepancy between a lengthy aquatic larval phase, which can occupy most of the year, and an extremely brief terrestrial adult stage reflects a life history heavily optimized for exploiting a narrow but predictable environmental window for reproductive activity typical of many heptageniid mayflies in temperate zones.
